scope_note: A sourced comparison of vector databases, purpose-built agent-memory frameworks, and graph-based memory systems — what actually works for episodic recall across a conversation, not generic RAG-benchmark scoring. This project runs no retrieval benchmarks of its own; scale and performance claims are attributed and marked accordingly.
method_note: Every claim is checked against the vendor's own documentation or source repository before publication, then adversarially audited in a second pass that actively tries to refute each field rather than confirm it, followed by a dedicated facet-recheck pass verifying every facet against the row's own (possibly-corrected) text. Scale/performance figures are mostly vendor-reported and marked verification: vendor-claim unless independently confirmed.

systems.name: Chroma
systems.price_note: Self-hosted OSS is free. Chroma Cloud (GA August 2025): $0/mo Starter + $5 credit, then $2.50/GiB written, $0.33/GiB-mo stored, $0.0075/TiB queried, $0.09/GiB egress; Team $250/mo; Enterprise custom.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: One HNSW ANN index per collection (cosine/L2/inner-product) in single-node/OSS Chroma; metadata (`where`) and document-content (`where_document`, backed by SQLite FTS5 substring/regex matching) filtering can be combined with a vector query, but this is filtered vector search, not dense+sparse fusion. Chroma separately documents an official Hybrid Search feature (Reciprocal Rank Fusion over dense embeddings + sparse BM25/SPLADE vectors) via its newer Search API, published under the Chroma Cloud docs (docs.trychroma.com/cloud/search-api/hybrid-search); self-hosted/OSS availability of this specific feature is not confirmed from public docs.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted single-node OSS, or managed via Chroma Cloud (distributed, serverless, on object storage).
systems.best_for: Prototyping and small-to-mid RAG apps that want the simplest embed-and-query API, with a clear upgrade path to a managed cloud once it outgrows one machine.
systems.watch: The open-source single-node engine keeps its entire HNSW index in system RAM, and Chroma's own docs confirm insert/query latency degrades once a collection approaches available memory. There is no fixed vector-count ceiling, though: capacity scales roughly linearly with RAM (~0.245M vectors per GB per Chroma's own formula), and Chroma's docs demonstrate ~15M vectors on a 64GB box with no strict upper bound found in testing. '5-10M vectors' is a rough community rule of thumb for typical 16-32GB hardware, not a hard limit. Once a single box's RAM is exhausted you need Chroma Cloud, a separate, newer, distributed engine (SPANN/SPFresh over object storage).
systems.standout: Ships with a default local embedding function (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 via onnxruntime), so you can go from raw text to a queryable collection with zero embedding-provider setup.
systems.embedding_model: Built-in default (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, local ONNX), with a pluggable embedding-function interface for OpenAI/Cohere/etc.
systems.scale_note: Chroma's own current docs give a linear RAM-based capacity formula for single-node OSS (~0.245M vectors per GB of RAM), demonstrate ~15M vectors on a 64GB instance, and state they found no strict upper bound up to the ~7M vectors they stress-tested; their newer single-node guide advertises support 'approaching tens of millions of embeddings' on adequate hardware. The often-cited '5-10M vector ceiling' is a rough community figure for common 16-32GB deployments, not Chroma's own stated hard limit. Chroma Cloud is a real distributed rearchitecture (SPANN/SPFresh index over object storage, per Chroma's engineering posts), though customer-facing sharding/replication controls are not detailed in public docs.
systems.integration: Python/JS clients; LangChain, LlamaIndex, and most agent-framework vector-store integrations.
systems.adoption: 29.0k GitHub stars (chroma-core/chroma, verified via GitHub API, Aug 2026); founded 2022, raised $18M seed in 2023.

systems.name: LanceDB
systems.price_note: OSS engine (embedded, self-host) is free; LanceDB Cloud is a usage-based serverless tier with no monthly minimum, still in public beta as of 2025.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: IVF-PQ, IVF-HNSW, and pure HNSW ANN indexes over the Lance columnar file format; built-in BM25 full-text index; hybrid search fuses vector + FTS with a reranker; supports pre/post-filter metadata pushdown and SQL WHERE-clause scans on scalar columns.
systems.self_host: Embedded-in-process (file-backed, no server to run) for self-hosting, or managed via LanceDB Cloud (public beta).
systems.best_for: Local-first or notebook-to-production RAG/multimodal search where you want a file-backed, serverless embedded store without running a database server.
systems.watch: LanceDB Cloud is still public beta (launched 2025) - most production workloads at real scale still run the OSS embedded engine self-managed; the managed/serverless story is newer and less battle-tested than Milvus/Qdrant/Pinecone's.
systems.standout: Built directly on the open Lance columnar file format (a Parquet-like format designed for random access + versioning), so the same files back both analytical (SQL/pandas/Arrow) and vector-search workloads with no ETL step.
systems.embedding_model: Bring-your-own via an embedding-function registry (OpenAI, Cohere, sentence-transformers, etc.); no default built-in model.
systems.scale_note: Vendor markets it for billions of vectors backed by object storage (S3/GCS/local disk); no independent large-scale benchmark verified here.
systems.integration: Python/JS/Rust SDKs; LangChain and LlamaIndex vector-store integrations.
systems.adoption: ~10k+ GitHub stars on lancedb/lancedb (company founded 2022, Series A funded).

systems.name: Marqo
systems.price_note: The open-source engine is deprecated with no further updates. The live Marqo product is a commercial, custom-quoted e-commerce search platform reached only via a sales/demo call - no self-serve pricing or signup is published. The specific billing basis (e.g. catalog size or traffic) is not stated anywhere on marqo.ai and could not be independently confirmed, so it should not be asserted.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: As it existed pre-deprecation: end-to-end vector search with automatic multimodal (text+image) embedding generation and HNSW-backed ANN retrieval.
systems.self_host: The open-source engine was self-hostable but is no longer maintained; the current commercial product is managed-only.
systems.best_for: Not recommended as a new choice for general-purpose vector search - historically useful for teams wanting embeddings generated automatically inside the database, but that project is now dead.
systems.watch: Marqo's GitHub repo carries an explicit deprecation notice ('Marqo's Open Source project is deprecated and will no longer receive updates') - the company pivoted from a general-purpose open-source vector database to a closed, e-commerce-specific commercial search/recommendation product. Anyone finding Marqo via an 'open-source vector database' roundup is looking at a dead project.
systems.standout: Was one of the earliest vector databases to make automatic multimodal embedding generation (text and images, no separate embedding step) the core of its API, before the open-source line was discontinued.

systems.name: Milvus
systems.price_note: Free self-hosted (including a lightweight embedded 'Milvus Lite' mode). Zilliz Cloud (managed): ~$0.096/CU-hour compute historically, with storage pricing reported to standardize at $0.04/GB/mo across major clouds from January 2026; also offers a serverless pay-as-you-go tier.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Selectable ANN index per collection - HNSW, IVF_FLAT/IVF_PQ/IVF_SQ8, DiskANN, GPU indexes, AUTOINDEX - plus SPARSE_INVERTED_INDEX for BM25; supports dense+sparse hybrid search and scalar metadata filtering.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted as a standalone binary, Docker container, or distributed Kubernetes cluster, or managed via Zilliz Cloud.
systems.best_for: Large-scale (100M+ vector) deployments that need a choice of ANN index algorithms and a distributed, horizontally-scaled architecture, self-hosted or managed.
systems.watch: The distributed self-hosted deployment (etcd + Pulsar/Kafka + object storage + multiple Milvus microservices) is a real operational commitment - teams that don't need billion-vector scale often find Milvus Lite or Zilliz Cloud a gentler entry point than standing up the full cluster topology themselves.
systems.standout: Lets you pick the ANN index per collection (HNSW for recall/speed, IVF for filtered-search-heavy workloads, DiskANN for datasets too large for RAM) instead of committing to one algorithm for the whole database.
systems.embedding_model: Bring-your-own; pymilvus ships optional 'Function' helpers (BM25 sparse, wrappers around external embedding providers) but requires your own API keys/models.
systems.scale_note: Milvus 2.6 (the generation this scale claim is based on) is marketed as scaling cost-effectively into the tens of billions of vectors; Milvus's own benchmark reports 90% recall at ~200ms median latency (50 concurrent queries, top-100) using VectorDBBench - a benchmark closely associated with the Zilliz/Milvus ecosystem, so treat as vendor-reported rather than independently confirmed. Note: Zilliz announced Milvus 3.0 in July 2026 - a 'lake-native' architecture (vector data left in open formats such as Lance/Iceberg/Parquet/Vortex on object storage, via a new 'Loon' storage engine) that is a materially different scaling/storage model from the 2.6 figures cited above; whether the tens-of-billions/VectorDBBench numbers have been re-validated under 3.0 could not be confirmed from available sources.
systems.integration: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack integrations; graduated to top-level Linux Foundation AI & Data project status in June 2021.
systems.adoption: 45.6k GitHub stars (milvus-io/milvus, verified via GitHub API, Aug 2026) and 100M+ downloads per Milvus's own count (vendor-claim).

systems.name: Pinecone
systems.price_note: Starter free tier; Builder $20/mo flat (new 2026 tier); Standard from $50/mo minimum (usage-based beyond that); Enterprise from $500/mo minimum with 99.95% SLA - billed on storage plus read/write 'units'.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Proprietary ANN search (serverless architecture; algorithm internals not published) across dense, sparse, and full-text index types in one service, with integrated metadata filtering and server-side reranking.
systems.self_host: Managed only (fully hosted SaaS). A 'Bring Your Own Cloud' enterprise option runs Pinecone in your cloud account but is still Pinecone-operated, not self-managed open source.
systems.best_for: Teams that want zero-ops vector search with usage-based serverless billing and have no need (or desire) to self-host anything.
systems.watch: There is no self-hosted or source-available option at all - Pinecone is 100% managed, so a compliance or air-gapped requirement that rules out sending data to a third-party service rules out Pinecone entirely (BYOC still means Pinecone's control plane touches your account).
systems.standout: Popularized 'vector database' as its own product category starting in 2019, and has leaned hardest into fully serverless usage-based billing, including a new low-cost 'Builder' flat tier introduced in 2026 aimed at solo developers.
systems.embedding_model: Built-in (Pinecone Inference: hosted embedding and reranking models) or bring-your-own vectors.
systems.scale_note: Vendor markets it for billions of vectors with idle serverless indexes costing nothing; no independent benchmark verified here.
systems.integration: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and most agent-framework connectors; REST/gRPC APIs with Python/JS/Go clients.
systems.adoption: No public repo/star count (proprietary); founded 2019 by Edo Liberty.

systems.name: Qdrant
systems.price_note: Free self-hosted. Cloud: Free tier (0.5 vCPU/1GB RAM/4GB disk); Standard tier billed hourly for provisioned resources (~$30-60/mo for a 2GB cluster per 2026 estimates); Premium adds SLA/SSO/private networking with a minimum spend; Hybrid Cloud (BYOC) is custom-priced.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: HNSW ANN index with an exact-search fallback; native sparse-vector support for dense+sparse hybrid search; payload (metadata) filters are compiled directly into the HNSW graph traversal rather than applied as a separate pre/post pass.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted (Docker/Kubernetes/binary) or managed via Qdrant Cloud, including a Hybrid Cloud/BYOC option.
systems.best_for: Teams that want a fast, single-purpose Rust vector engine with first-class filtered search and sparse+dense hybrid retrieval, self-hosted or in their own cloud.
systems.watch: Qdrant's client ships FastEmbed for local ONNX embedding generation - a client-side convenience, not a server feature, on self-hosted Qdrant (which also does server-side BM25 sparse-vector generation, but nothing dense). However, Qdrant Cloud (since July 2025) offers a managed 'Cloud Inference' feature that DOES generate dense/sparse/multimodal embeddings server-side for supported models (MiniLM, SPLADE, BM25, Mixedbread Embed-Large, CLIP) - so the 'server never embeds for you' distinction from Weaviate/Pinecone holds only for self-hosted OSS Qdrant, not for Qdrant Cloud.
systems.standout: Filters are compiled into the HNSW graph traversal itself instead of a pre/post-filter pass, which the project cites as why filtered search stays fast at high filter selectivity where naive pre/post-filtering on other engines slows down.
systems.embedding_model: Self-hosted: bring-your-own vectors, aside from server-side BM25 sparse-vector generation; optional client-side FastEmbed library (ONNX, default BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5) for local dense embedding generation. Qdrant Cloud additionally offers a managed 'Cloud Inference' service (since July 2025) that generates dense/sparse/multimodal embeddings server-side for supported models (MiniLM, SPLADE, BM25, Mixedbread Embed-Large, CLIP).
systems.scale_note: Vendor markets it for billion-vector scale via sharding/replication; no independent benchmark verified here.
systems.integration: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and most agent-framework connectors; gRPC/REST APIs with Python/JS/Rust/Go clients.
systems.adoption: 33.9k GitHub stars (qdrant/qdrant, verified via GitHub API, Aug 2026); founded 2021 in Berlin.

systems.name: Redis (Vector Sets / RediSearch)
systems.licence: Choice of RSALv2, SSPLv1, or AGPLv3 (tri-licensed as of Redis 8, May 2025)
systems.price_note: Redis Open Source (any of the three licenses) is free to self-host. Redis Cloud and Redis Software are separate closed-source commercial products requiring a license from Redis Ltd.; managed vector-search pricing not independently verified here.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Native Vector Sets data type (Redis 8+, VADD/VSIM commands) with automatic HNSW indexing (no separate index-creation step) and built-in int8/binary quantization; also the older RediSearch VECTOR field type (HNSW or FLAT/exact) with hybrid full-text + vector queries and secondary-index metadata filtering.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted under any of the three OSS license choices, or managed via Redis Cloud (a separate, closed-source commercial product) or cloud-provider offerings like Azure Managed Redis / GCP Memorystore for Redis.
systems.best_for: Teams already running Redis for caching/session state who want to add vector similarity to the same in-memory store rather than stand up a separate vector database, especially where quantized (int8/binary) vectors fit comfortably in RAM.
systems.watch: Only AGPLv3 (one of the three license choices) is OSI-approved open source - RSALv2 and SSPLv1 explicitly forbid offering Redis itself as a competing managed service. The license history is genuinely tangled: BSD-3-Clause through v7.2, then RSAL/SSPL-only for v7.4-7.8 (open-source status dropped entirely in March 2024), before AGPLv3 was added back as a third option in Redis 8 (May 2025). Don't assume 'Redis is open source' the way it was before 2024 without checking which license you're actually under.
systems.standout: Vector Sets (the new Redis 8 data type) turn on HNSW indexing automatically with no schema/index-creation step and ship int8 and binary quantization built in - Redis's own benchmark reports ~50,000 VSIM operations/sec on a single host with default int8 quantization.
systems.embedding_model: Bring-your-own only - Redis stores and indexes vectors but does not generate embeddings itself.
systems.scale_note: Redis's own benchmark reports ~50,000 VSIM operations/sec on a single host for a multi-million-item, 300-dimension vector set using default int8 quantization; being in-memory, practical dataset size is bounded by available RAM (quantization reduces this significantly).
systems.integration: RedisVL, LangChain, and LlamaIndex integrations; also available as a managed vector store via AWS/GCP/Azure Redis offerings.
systems.released: RediSearch vector support ~2022 (Vector Similarity Search shipped in RediSearch 2.4, GA March 2022); Vector Sets data type introduced in Redis 8 (2025)

systems.name: Turbopuffer
systems.price_note: Usage-based across three tiers: Launch (from ~$16-64/mo depending on source), Scale ($256/mo, adds HIPAA BAA/SSO/priority support), Enterprise (from $4,096+/mo, single-tenancy/BYOC/CMEK/99.95% SLA). Storage from ~$0.02/GB (~$70/TB-mo published); queries billed at $1/PB scanned (cut from $5/PB in February 2026); an April 2026 'namespace pinning' option lets high-QPS namespaces pay GB-hours for reserved hot capacity instead.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: ANN vector search plus native BM25 full-text search in one engine, combinable as hybrid search; built on a three-tier cache (object storage -> NVMe -> RAM) rather than an always-in-RAM index; supports metadata filtering and ranking.
systems.self_host: Managed only. The Enterprise tier offers BYOC (bring-your-own-cloud), but it remains Turbopuffer-operated, not a self-hostable open-source binary.
systems.best_for: High-namespace-count, cost-sensitive multi-tenant workloads (e.g. per-user or per-document search) where most data is queried rarely and you don't want to pay to keep it hot in RAM at all times.
systems.watch: The pricing model is genuinely novel (pay mostly for what you query, near-zero for cold/inactive namespaces), but that means cost is workload-shaped rather than a flat per-GB number - a namespace with sustained high QPS needs the newer (April 2026) namespace-pinning add-on or the per-query-scan cost can dominate the bill.
systems.standout: Built from scratch on object storage (S3/GCS) as the source of truth rather than keeping the full index resident in RAM/SSD - the architecture bet that lets it charge near-zero for inactive tenants, and reportedly the search backend behind Cursor, Notion, and (per its own materials) Anthropic.
systems.embedding_model: Bring-your-own only - a pure vector + full-text store with no embedding generation.
systems.scale_note: Object-storage-backed architecture is marketed as removing practical per-namespace size limits; adoption by Cursor, Notion, and Anthropic (per Turbopuffer's own press/case-study material) is the strongest available evidence of real production scale, though exact vector counts aren't published.
systems.integration: REST API with official clients; publicly reported as the search backend inside Cursor and Notion.
systems.adoption: Customers reported to include Cursor, Notion, and Anthropic (per Turbopuffer's own press materials and third-party reporting, including a Google Cloud case study - vendor-claim, not independently audited); independently reported to have reached roughly a $100M annualized revenue run-rate by March 2026 (up from ~$75M at end of 2025), remaining profitable on well under $1M raised.

systems.name: Vald
systems.price_note: Free, open-source; no managed cloud offering - cost is whatever Kubernetes infrastructure you run it on.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Distributed ANN search using NGT (Neighborhood Graph and Tree, developed by Yahoo Japan) as the default index algorithm, with automatic indexing, index backup, and auto-healing across a Kubernetes-native microservice architecture.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted only, Kubernetes-native (Helm charts); no managed/hosted option.
systems.best_for: Teams already running Kubernetes who want a horizontally-scaled, auto-healing ANN search layer that scales with the cluster rather than a monolithic vector database process.
systems.watch: There is no managed cloud and no lightweight single-binary mode - Vald's microservices-on-Kubernetes architecture is close to mandatory, making it a heavier operational commitment than Qdrant's or Milvus's simpler single-node deployment options for teams not already on K8s.
systems.standout: Uses NGT rather than the HNSW/IVF family most other engines default to, and is built specifically as a set of Kubernetes microservices (not a single database process in a container) with built-in auto-healing and automatic index backup.
systems.embedding_model: Bring-your-own only - Vald is a pure ANN search engine with no embedding generation.
systems.scale_note: Vendor markets it for horizontal scaling to billions of feature vectors via Kubernetes cluster scale-out; no independent benchmark verified here.
systems.integration: gRPC APIs with clients in Go, Python, Java, Node.js; Kubernetes/Helm-native deployment; listed on the CNCF Landscape.
systems.adoption: ~1.7k GitHub stars - a much smaller community than Milvus/Qdrant/Weaviate.
systems.released: ~2019 (project origin); latest release v1.7.17, published July 4, 2025 — a v1.8.0 release was merging as of early August 2026

systems.name: Vectara
systems.licence: Proprietary platform (no source available); an open-source MCP client integration, vectara-mcp, exists separately under an open license
systems.price_note: Free 30-day trial with nearly all enterprise features. Enterprise deployment-tier list pricing confirmed directly on vectara.com/pricing: SaaS from $100K/yr, VPC from $250K/yr, on-prem from $500K/yr - this is contact-sales enterprise-contract pricing, not a published self-serve plan. Third-party resellers (e.g. a 2025-dated pricing aggregator) report a legacy self-serve overage rate of roughly $7.50/mo per +5MB account size/+1,000 queries, but this figure does not appear on Vectara's current public pricing page and could not be independently confirmed as still active - treat as unverified.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Managed end-to-end RAG pipeline (ingest -> embed -> retrieve -> generate) rather than exposed raw ANN parameters; supports 'Bring Your Own Model' for embeddings/generation alongside its own proprietary Boomerang (retrieval) and Mockingbird (generation) models.
systems.self_host: Managed SaaS by default; VPC and on-premise deployment tiers exist but at enterprise contract pricing, not as a self-hosted open-source binary.
systems.best_for: Enterprises that want a turnkey, governed RAG platform (retrieval + hallucination detection + generation) as one contracted service, rather than assembling a vector store and pipeline themselves.
systems.watch: This is not a raw vector database in the sense the other rows are - there's no direct ANN/index-tuning control, self-hosting is an enterprise contract line item (quoted from ~$250K/yr for VPC), and the entry-level pricing shown publicly ($7.50 per small overage bundle) is not representative of what a real deployment costs.
systems.standout: Bundles hallucination detection and 'always-on governance' directly into the retrieval pipeline rather than leaving that to the caller, positioning itself as a full RAG platform rather than a retrieval building block.
systems.embedding_model: Built-in (proprietary Boomerang retrieval model), or bring-your-own embedding/generation models.
systems.scale_note: No independently verifiable scale figures found; the enterprise deployment-tier pricing ($100K-500K+/yr) is the clearest available signal of intended scale.
systems.integration: LangChain vectorstore integration; an open-source MCP server (vectara-mcp) for agent/tool-use access.

systems.name: Vespa
systems.price_note: Free, self-hosted OSS engine. Vespa Cloud (managed) publishes per-unit hourly pricing (vCPU/memory/disk) across four tiers (Startup/Basic/Commercial/Enterprise) on its price calculator (cloud.vespa.ai/price-calculator); the separate 'Self Managed' support tier is contact-sales only, and the Enterprise tier carries a $20,000/month minimum.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Combines dense-vector ANN (HNSW), sparse/keyword (BM25-style) text ranking, structured filters, geospatial queries, and machine-learned ranking in one query, including multi-vector-per-document retrieval for ColBERT/ColPali-style late-interaction search.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted (own infrastructure) or managed via Vespa Cloud (including on AWS).
systems.best_for: Large-scale production search/recommendation systems that need to combine vector, keyword, structured, and ML-ranked retrieval in a single engine rather than bolting vector search onto a separate index.
systems.watch: Vespa's power comes from real operational depth - its own query language, ranking-expression system, and cluster topology - so teams evaluating it purely as 'a vector database' often underestimate the learning curve versus a narrower ANN-only engine.
systems.standout: Built at Yahoo on technology descended from FAST (open-sourced 2017); spun out in October 2023 as an independent company (Vespa.ai), with Yahoo retaining an investor stake, a board seat, and its status as largest customer. The same engine runs Yahoo Mail's RAG pipeline and Spotify's recommendation serving, giving it production pedigree at a scale most vector-only databases haven't been proven at.
systems.embedding_model: Supports running embedding inference (e.g. Hugging Face models) inside the engine itself, or bring-your-own precomputed vectors.
systems.scale_note: Vespa's own materials claim <100ms latency at billion-scale retrieval, with no specific figure published for that scale. A third-party 2026 vector-DB comparison cites Vespa at ~15ms p99 latency, but that figure is from a 10M-vector benchmark, not billion-scale as sometimes implied. Production use at Yahoo Mail (RAG) and Spotify (recommendations) is real but vendor/case-study reported, not independently benchmarked here.
systems.integration: LangChain and LlamaIndex integrations exist; native Java/Python plugin and query-language APIs.
systems.adoption: Production use cited at Yahoo and Spotify (per Vespa's own case studies - vendor-claim).
systems.released: 2017 (open-sourced by Yahoo). Traces to Fast Search & Transfer (FAST), a Norwegian search company founded 1997 (alltheweb.com), which Yahoo acquired via its 2003 acquisition of Overture Services.

systems.name: Weaviate
systems.price_note: Free self-hosted. Weaviate Cloud is metered on vector dimensions stored/month, but the tier structure changed in an October 2025 pricing update: the old "Serverless Cloud" and "Enterprise Cloud" tiers were renamed "Shared Cloud" and "Dedicated Cloud." Weaviate's own current pricing page (weaviate.io/pricing, checked 2026) lists Flex (from $45/mo) at ~$0.00465/1M dimensions, and Premium at ~$0.003875/1M dimensions (Shared deployment) or ~$0.002718/1M dimensions (Dedicated deployment) — list rates vary by cloud provider/region. The ~$0.095/1M-dimension figure widely repeated on third-party sites reflects the pre-October-2025 pricing structure and could not be confirmed on Weaviate's current page.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: HNSW ANN index (plus a flat/brute-force index option for small collections); native BM25 keyword scoring fused with vector distance for hybrid search; structured property filtering.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted (Docker/Kubernetes/Helm) or managed via Weaviate Cloud — Free, Flex, or Premium tiers, with Premium offering Shared or Dedicated deployment (the older "Enterprise Cloud"/BYOC naming was retired in Weaviate's October 2025 pricing restructure; current BYOC availability was not independently confirmed).
systems.best_for: Teams that want the database itself to own embedding generation (via built-in vectorizer modules) alongside combined vector+keyword hybrid search, self-hosted or managed.
systems.watch: Cloud pricing bills on vector dimensions x count, not raw vector count or GB - two collections with identical vector counts can cost very differently depending on the embedding model's dimensionality, so the cost surprise shows up after picking an embedding model, not before.
systems.standout: Pluggable vectorizer modules (text2vec-openai, text2vec-transformers, multi2vec-clip, etc.) let the database itself call the embedding model at ingest and query time, removing the need for a separate embedding pipeline.
systems.embedding_model: Built-in via pluggable vectorizer modules (OpenAI, Cohere, HuggingFace/transformers, CLIP, etc.), or bring-your-own precomputed vectors.
systems.scale_note: Vendor markets it as cloud-native and horizontally scalable; no independent benchmark verified here.
systems.integration: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack integrations; GraphQL and REST/gRPC APIs.
systems.adoption: ~16k+ GitHub stars; founded 2019.

systems.name: pgvector
systems.price_note: Free, open-source Postgres extension - cost is whatever Postgres hosting you already pay for (self-managed, RDS, Supabase, Neon, etc.); no separate vector-db bill.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Exact (brute-force) search plus two ANN index types - IVFFlat (faster build, less memory, lower recall/speed) and HNSW (slower build, more memory, better recall/speed) - combinable with ordinary SQL WHERE clauses for metadata filtering, and with Postgres full-text search for hybrid queries.
systems.self_host: Self-hosted only, as a Postgres extension - inherits whichever Postgres hosting model you already use, including managed Postgres providers.
systems.best_for: Teams that already run Postgres and want vector search as one more column type/index inside their existing database, transactions, and access-control model, rather than a second system to operate.
systems.watch: It's bounded by single-instance Postgres - engineering-blog consensus puts noticeable query degradation starting around 10-20M vectors on one node (the pgvectorscale extension pushes that toward ~50M), and HNSW index builds on large datasets can take hours and multiple times the dataset size in memory. Past that, teams typically add a dedicated vector database rather than keep scaling one Postgres box.
systems.standout: Because it's a native Postgres type, vector similarity can be combined with ACID transactions, row-level security, and arbitrary relational joins in a single SQL query - no separate consistency model to reconcile between two databases.
systems.embedding_model: Bring-your-own only - pgvector stores and indexes vectors but has no embedding-generation feature itself.
systems.scale_note: Community/engineering-blog consensus (not an official pgvector benchmark) puts noticeable degradation starting around 10-20M vectors on a single node, with the pgvectorscale extension pushing that toward ~50M.
systems.integration: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and virtually every Postgres-compatible ORM/framework; works anywhere Postgres runs (RDS, Supabase, Neon, Timescale, self-hosted).
systems.adoption: ~22k+ GitHub stars; created by Andrew Kane, first released April 2021.

systems.name: Cognee
systems.price_note: OSS self-host: free forever, per vendor ('run the full memory engine locally or on your own stack'). Cloud: Free (1,000,000 tokens included, 1 workspace, no card required, unlimited users/API calls) → Standard $2.50 per 1M tokens processed (unlimited workspaces, $5/extra workspace/mo, Slack/Notion/Google Drive connectors) → custom Enterprise (dedicated support engineer, BYOC, SLA). Note: some third-party listings cite additional 'Developer $35/mo' and 'Team $200/mo' tiers, but these could not be confirmed on the official cognee.ai/pricing page as of this research and are omitted here as unverified.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Auto-routes each query via a rule-based (not LLM-based) router, on by default, choosing among strategies that blend vector similarity with graph structure/traversal; recall() defaults to graph-based retrieval rather than plain embedding similarity for permanent memory. Graph storage defaults to an embedded Kuzu-compatible engine (provider 'ladybug'), NOT Neo4j — Neo4j, Postgres, and Amazon Neptune are supported alternative graph backends. Vector store defaults to LanceDB, with pgvector and ChromaDB built in and Qdrant/Weaviate/Milvus/Redis/FalkorDB available via community adapters.
systems.self_host: Yes — fully self-hostable, Apache-2.0, Python 3.10+.
systems.best_for: Teams wanting a self-hosted, graph-native memory engine with an explicit forget/re-weighting loop and broad first-party data-source ingestion (Slack/Notion/Drive).
systems.watch: forget() is selective, not dataset-only: it supports item-level (data_id), dataset-level, memory-only, and account-wide scopes. An opt-in 'Detect contradictions' task exists in the cognify pipeline (off by default), but it's undocumented whether it resolves conflicts or only flags them — Cognee's own guidance still recommends manual replacement of outdated facts. No automatic decay/aging-out of stale facts is documented either way.
systems.standout: Not the only system here with memory-lifecycle controls - mem0, elsewhere in this catalog, already ships an explicit delete()/delete_all() API plus a named Memory Decay feature that continuously down-weights a stale memory's relevance by recency. What stays distinct about Cognee is its forget() granularity (item-level, dataset-level, memory-only, or account-wide) and a re-weighting loop that considers importance, frequency, and feedback together, not recency alone.
systems.memory_policy: Every input runs through cognee's ECL pipeline: remember() (add + cognify + improve) is the macro flow, and 'cognify' itself decomposes into six ordered tasks (classify documents, check permissions, extract chunks, extract graph, summarize text, add data points) feeding a hybrid graph + vector + relational store, so one 'memory' is simultaneously a graph node, an embedding, and a relational row. Docs describe an opt-in 'Detect contradictions' task (CONTRADICTION_DETECTION=true, off by default) in that pipeline, but it is undocumented whether it resolves conflicts or only flags them — Cognee's own tutorial content still recommends manually replacing an outdated fact rather than relying on automatic resolution. No automatic decay/aging-out of stale facts is documented. forget() IS selective, contrary to earlier reporting: it supports item-level deletion (forget(data_id=..., dataset=...)), dataset-level, memory-only (keeps raw files), and account-wide (forget(everything=True)) scopes.
systems.embedding_model: Pluggable via LiteLLM across seven+ LLM/embedding providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Ollama, and others); defaults to nomic-embed-text (via Ollama) or all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (via Fastembed, CPU-only) depending on setup.
systems.scale_note: Vendor claims only (Feb 2026 seed announcement): 1M+ pipeline runs, 500x YoY growth, 70+ production deployments. Self-reported and not independently verified. No independent benchmark of these figures, or of Cognee's conflict-resolution accuracy, was found in the literature.
systems.integration: REST API plus Python/TypeScript SDKs; an MCP server for agentic tool use (Claude, Codex); 28+ built-in data-source ingestion connectors.
systems.adoption: 29.8k GitHub stars (topoteretes/cognee, verified via direct repo fetch, Aug 2026), 80+ contributors; $7.5M seed round (February 2026, led by Pebblebed).
systems.released: Repository history dates to August 2023; company (Topoteretes, Berlin) founded 2024 by Boris Arzentar and Vasilije Markovic; 'cognee v1' platform launched 2026.

systems.name: LangMem (LangGraph long-term memory)
systems.price_note: No pricing — MIT-licensed open-source Python SDK only; no hosted product or managed service exists for LangMem itself. Cost is entirely whatever LLM, embedding, and storage backend (e.g., self-hosted Postgres, or the separately-priced LangGraph Platform) you attach to it.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Two memory-formation modes, an explicit developer trade-off: hot-path (the agent calls create_manage_memory_tool/create_search_memory_tool in-line during the conversation, giving immediate availability at the cost of added latency) or background (an async memory manager extracts/consolidates/updates after the fact, on a schedule or manual trigger). Three memory types are distinguished — semantic (facts, stored as either an update-in-place 'profile' object or an append-only 'collection'), episodic (past agent actions/experiences), and procedural (system prompts/instructions).
systems.self_host: Yes by construction — it is a library (MIT), not a hosted service. Core primitives work with any storage backend implementing LangGraph's BaseStore interface (in-memory, Postgres, Redis, etc.); there is no separate self-host deployment step because there is no server component to run.
systems.best_for: Teams already committed to LangGraph who want first-party long-term memory (semantic/episodic/procedural) without adding a separate memory service — a weak fit if the agent framework is undecided or is not LangChain/LangGraph.
systems.watch: Positioned by LangChain primarily as the long-term-memory companion to LangGraph — native integration with LangGraph's storage layer is the emphasized path in docs and tutorials, even though the core memory-management primitives are documented as usable standalone with any storage backend. Release cadence has slowed: the latest PyPI release is 0.0.30 from October 27, 2025 (still pre-1.0), even though the GitHub repo shows commit activity into mid-2026 — treat it as actively developed but not yet a stable, versioned API. No forgetting or decay mechanism is documented for long-term storage; LangChain's own guidance addresses removing stale information only for the short-term (in-context) window, not the persistent store.
systems.standout: Splits memory into semantic/episodic/procedural types with distinct extraction strategies (profile-style vs. collection-style) and offers both a hot-path (in-loop) and background (async) memory-formation mode as an explicit, documented trade-off — most competitors in this category pick one mode silently.
systems.memory_policy: Developer-chosen extraction timing (hot-path in-conversation tool calls vs. an async background manager) and developer-chosen storage shape per memory type: semantic facts can be stored as an update-in-place 'profile' object (overwritten on conflict) or an append-only 'collection' (old and new both kept); episodic and procedural memory follow the same two-mode split. No forgetting or decay mechanism is documented for the persistent long-term store — LangChain's own guidance only addresses trimming the short-term, in-context window, not what has already been written to long-term storage.
systems.embedding_model: None built in — bring your own embeddings model via whichever LangGraph-compatible BaseStore/vector index you configure; works with any embedding provider that store supports.
systems.scale_note: Reported download counts (746K monthly / 5M+ total, per a third-party aggregator) versus a comparatively small 1.6k GitHub star count suggest most installs are transitive (via LangChain/LangGraph) rather than deliberate adoption of LangMem specifically — flagged here rather than presented as a clean adoption signal.
systems.integration: Native integration with LangGraph's long-term memory Store API; framework-agnostic core primitives (any BaseStore) exist, but documentation, tutorials, and adoption are centered on the LangChain/LangGraph ecosystem.
systems.adoption: ~1.6k GitHub stars (langchain-ai/langmem); one third-party aggregator reports ~746K monthly / 5M+ total PyPI downloads (not independently cross-checked against PyPI's own stats) — the gap between modest stars and large reported install counts likely reflects transitive installation via LangChain/LangGraph tutorials rather than deliberate LangMem-specific adoption.
systems.released: First released as the open-source LangMem SDK in early 2025 (GitHub repo created Jan 21, 2025; public launch blog post Feb 18, 2025, announcing 'pip install -U langmem'). Builds on LangGraph's native long-term memory support (BaseStore primitives), which launched separately in October 2024, and an earlier hosted 'LangMem' alpha service of undocumented launch date — neither of those is the OSS SDK itself. Latest release v0.0.30 on October 27, 2025 (package remains pre-1.0).

systems.name: Letta
systems.price_note: OSS self-host: free (Apache-2.0). Cloud: Free tier (limited managed agents, bring-your-own API keys) → Pro $20/mo (up to 20 stateful agents plus a Letta Auto quota, pay-as-you-go overage) → API plan $20/mo base + $0.10/active-agent/mo + $0.00015/sec tool execution (for fleets of many long-lived agents) → Teams Pro $20/seat/mo → custom Enterprise (RBAC, SAML/OIDC SSO, volume pricing).
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Letta Code's current memory system (Context Repositories / MemFS) stores agent memory as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in a git repo that is cloned to the local filesystem and kept in sync. Files under system/ load into the agent's system prompt every turn; everything else stays discoverable via the memory tree (folder hierarchy, filenames, frontmatter descriptions) but its full contents load only when the agent reads it. There is no dedicated memory-editing tool call (the old core_memory_replace-style API) — the agent reads and writes memory using normal filesystem/bash tools (ls, grep, cat, custom scripts), and every edit is committed to the MemFS git repo, giving memory real version history and conflict resolution. Docs state explicitly that MemFS does not include a semantic or vector index by default — agents find memory via normal file-search and read tools. Because it's a git repo, multiple subagents can edit memory concurrently in isolated git worktrees and merge back.
systems.self_host: Current guidance (docs.letta.com/self-hosting) is built around the 'App Server,' not the legacy Docker+Postgres server. Two supported modes: local runtime (the agent runs in-process via the CLI or desktop app, storing state on local disk, no server required) or a self-hosted App Server (a standalone always-on service exposing agents to multiple clients via the Agent SDK, with capability-token or signed-bearer-token auth). Requires Node.js 22.19+. No Postgres/pgvector needed for this path. Docs warn the App Server has filesystem and shell access on its host and must never be exposed directly to untrusted clients.
systems.best_for: Letta Code launched (April 2026) explicitly framed as 'a memory-first coding agent' and is still primarily marketed and benchmarked in that role (topped Terminal-Bench among open-source coding agents, March 2026). Its README has since broadened the framing to a general-purpose 'stateful agent harness' usable for always-on agents over Slack, Telegram, and Discord — but the product name, primary distribution (npm CLI), and public benchmarking remain coding-agent-centric. Best suited today for developers wanting a coding-agent harness with durable, git-versioned memory across sessions; general-purpose stateful-agent use is a secondary, less-proven framing.
systems.watch: Memory hygiene is opt-in, not automatic: without explicitly enabling the optional background 'dreaming' subagent or invoking the 'memory doctor' skill, nothing reconciles, decays, or prunes stored memory on its own — quality depends entirely on the primary agent's own file edits. Absorbed MemGPT: the original MemGPT open-source codebase and team became Letta in the September 2024 rebrand — 'MemGPT' now refers only to the original research paper/technique, not a separately maintained current product, so do not treat MemGPT as a distinct living system.
systems.standout: Memory is a git repository, not a database record, so multiple subagents can edit it concurrently in isolated git worktrees and merge changes back — giving agent memory diff/history/conflict-resolution semantics instead of sequential memory-tool calls.
systems.memory_policy: Still no automatic decay, pruning, or silent forgetting of stored memory. Memory hygiene is not purely reactive to agent tool calls, though: Letta Code supports an optional, configurable background 'dreaming' subagent (triggered by message count or context-window compaction) that reviews recent conversation and commits consolidated updates to the git memory repo, working in its own git worktree and merging back automatically. A separate 'memory doctor' skill can also be invoked to reorganize a memory hierarchy that has grown messy. Both are deliberate, configured mechanisms, not silent automatic reconciliation.
systems.embedding_model: None required by default — MemFS/Context Repositories are purely file- and git-based, with no semantic or vector index; agents locate memory with standard file-search and read tools. An optional 'MemFS Search' mod can add semantic/hybrid search via a separate indexing tool if installed, but this is opt-in, not core to the architecture.
systems.scale_note: No vendor-published scale figures exist for the current MemFS/Context Repository architecture — unlike a vector index, capacity is bounded by git-repo size and how much a subagent can usefully hold in its memory tree, not a stated interactions-per-agent ceiling. A 'potentially millions of stored interactions' figure sometimes cited for Letta refers to the superseded Postgres+pgvector legacy server, not the current MemFS-based product.
systems.integration: Own agent runtime (Agent Development Environment) plus REST API and SDKs; agents can be called as tools/endpoints from other orchestrators (including LangGraph), and ship with a Slack app and desktop client.
systems.adoption: 23.9k+ GitHub stars on the core framework (letta-ai/letta — now labeled the legacy server by the vendor) plus roughly 2.8k-3k on the newer 'Letta Code' harness (letta-ai/letta-code), as of mid-2026. $10M seed funding (announced September 23, 2024, ~$70M post-money valuation) led by Felicis Ventures, with Sunflower Capital and Essence VC, plus angel investors including Jeff Dean and Clem Delangue. No source found supporting Founders Fund or Y Combinator participation as the original row claimed — likely fabricated.
systems.released: MemGPT research paper published October 2023 (UC Berkeley); the MemGPT open-source project and team rebranded and relaunched as Letta on September 23, 2024.
systems.verification_note: retrieval_mechanics/self_host/best_for/embedding_model/standout/memory_policy/scale_note/watch verified directly against docs.letta.com/self-hosting, docs.letta.com/concepts/memfs, docs.letta.com/letta-agent/memory, letta.com/blog posts, and the current letta-ai/letta + letta-ai/letta-code READMEs (Aug 2026), after the initial research pass was found to describe the superseded legacy server. A whole-branch review caught two of those fields (scale_note, part of watch) still describing the legacy Postgres+pgvector server after the first correction pass; both were rewritten to match the rest of the row.

systems.name: Zep
systems.licence: Proprietary (Zep Cloud/Enterprise); the underlying Graphiti engine is Apache-2.0
systems.price_note: No self-host option for Zep itself. Free tier (10,000 credits/mo, no rollover, 2 projects) → Flex $104/mo or $1,250/yr (50,000 credits/mo, 5 projects, 600 req/min) → Flex Plus $312/mo or $3,750/yr (200,000 credits/mo, 10 projects, observations/webhooks/analytics) → 'Emerging Companies' $13,000/yr (adds SOC 2 II, HIPAA BAA, BYOK) → custom Enterprise (BYOC/VPC, guaranteed SLA). Credits: 1 per ~350-byte ingested episode; retrieval, storage, threads and users are free.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Every ingested message is processed by the Graphiti engine into a per-user temporal knowledge graph: an LLM extracts entities/relationships/facts and resolves them against existing graph nodes; on contradiction, the prior edge's validity window is closed (invalid_at set to the new fact's valid_at) rather than deleted — a bi-temporal model recording both valid-time and transaction-time on every edge. Retrieval combines graph traversal with semantic/hybrid search over the graph. Conversation 'Threads' (sessions) by default all feed into a single persistent per-user 'User Graph' — there is no isolated ephemeral-session tier by default.
systems.self_host: No supported self-host path as of Aug 2026. Zep Community Edition (the former self-hostable server) was discontinued and moved to a legacy/ folder — remains Apache-2.0 but frozen, with no further updates or support. Current Zep is cloud-only; Enterprise adds BYOK or BYOC (bring-your-own-cloud/VPC) deployment of the closed-source service, which is not the same as open self-hosting. The underlying temporal-graph engine, Graphiti, is separately open-source (Apache-2.0, actively maintained, ~24.9k GitHub stars) and can be self-hosted standalone, but it is a graph-construction engine, not a drop-in replacement for Zep's session/user memory management, ingestion pipeline, or product surface.
systems.best_for: Teams whose retrieval questions are inherently temporal ('what was true, and when' / 'has this changed'), and who are comfortable depending on a cloud-only (or BYOC-Enterprise) service in exchange for the most rigorous bi-temporal fact-tracking in this category.
systems.watch: No supported self-host route — evaluate the cloud/BYOC dependency explicitly before committing, and note the free/Flex tiers have no rollover and are rate-limited under load. Fact invalidation preserves superseded facts rather than deleting them, and no decay or pruning policy is documented, so the graph is architecturally append-only at the storage layer even though queries surface only current facts — verify long-horizon storage-growth cost before committing at scale. Zep's own comparative benchmark numbers against Mem0 are self-published on Zep's blog, not third-party audited.
systems.standout: A bi-temporal fact graph (valid-time AND transaction-time on every edge) is the most rigorous approach in this category to 'what changed and when' — it supersedes rather than overwrites, so history stays queryable even as current-state answers stay accurate.
systems.memory_policy: Bi-temporal: every fact-graph edge carries both valid-time (when the fact was true in the world) and transaction-time (when it was ingested/superseded). A new message is checked against existing graph edges via the Graphiti engine; on contradiction, the prior edge is not deleted but has its validity window closed (invalid_at set to the new fact's valid_at), so the graph can answer 'what was believed and when' rather than only 'what is true now.' No decay or pruning policy is documented — invalidated edges persist as history forever, making storage architecturally append-only even though queries surface only current facts.
systems.embedding_model: Entity-node embeddings are managed internally (~1024-dimensional) in the hosted product, not user-configurable there. The open-source Graphiti engine underneath is pluggable: OpenAI (default), Voyage, Google Gemini, and Sentence Transformers embeddings are supported, plus local models via Ollama.
systems.scale_note: Zep's own LoCoMo figures have shifted across posts and are actively disputed, not settled: Zep's original claim (~84%) was challenged by Mem0's co-founder in a GitHub issue (getzep/zep-papers#5, closed 2025-05-19 by Zep's own founder citing inactivity, with no agreement reached between the two teams), alleging a calculation error (adversarial-category questions included in the numerator but excluded from the denominator) that inflated the score by ~25 points versus a corrected 58.44%. Zep's own rebuttal post ('Is Mem0 Really SOTA in Agent Memory?') instead states 75.14% +/-0.17 at 632ms p95 latency -- not the 80.32%/189ms figure originally reported here, which could not be traced to any primary Zep source and should be treated as unverified. On LongMemEval, Zep reports 63.8% vs. a cited 49.0% for Mem0 (GPT-4o), a figure corroborated by several independent comparison sites though not confirmed directly from a Zep primary post. Treat all of these as unaudited vendor claims inside an active, disputed benchmark war, not as settled numbers.
systems.integration: REST API plus Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs; documented framework integrations for LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen.
systems.adoption: Graphiti engine: GitHub star count is stale in the original figure (~24.9k) -- the project has grown rapidly and third-party citations put it at roughly 27-29k as of mid-2026; check github.com/getzep/graphiti directly rather than relying on a fixed number. Company funding/revenue figures conflict and are incomplete across sources: one source reports ~$1M revenue with no VC funding; Crunchbase/Y Combinator report a $500K pre-seed round (5 Mar 2024, YC-led); a separate source (fundz.net) reports an uncorroborated $1.8M seed round dated 27 Dec 2023; PitchBook and CB Insights report $2.3M total raised across 3 rounds. Treat all company-scale figures as unverified pending a primary source.
systems.released: Company founded 2023 by Daniel Chalef (the specific founding month, sometimes cited as May 2023, is not independently confirmed from a primary source). Zep Community Edition (OSS, self-hostable) launched 2023 and was deprecated/discontinued around April 2025 per Zep's own announcement, with the code moved to a legacy/ folder. Graphiti was open-sourced separately; the bi-temporal knowledge-graph architecture is described in the paper 'Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory' (arXiv:2501.13956), published 20 Jan 2025 -- no source found uses the label 'Zep v3' for this architecture.

systems.name: mem0
systems.price_note: OSS self-host: free (Apache-2.0), unlimited, run entirely on your own infra. Hosted Platform: Hobby free (10,000 add requests/mo, 1,000 retrieval requests/mo, 1 project) → Starter $19/mo (50,000/5,000) → Pro $249/mo (500,000/50,000, unlimited projects, graph memory, memory consolidation) → custom Enterprise (unlimited, on-prem, SSO, audit logs).
systems.retrieval_mechanics: LLM-based fact extraction over conversation turns writes into a vector store (Qdrant default; Chroma, pgvector, Redis, FAISS, Weaviate, Milvus, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Supabase, Azure AI Search, Upstash, S3 Vectors, Databricks, Turbopuffer and more are pluggable) with an optional graph-memory layer for entity linking. Retrieval is 'multi-signal': semantic vector search + BM25 keyword + entity matching, scoped by user_id/agent_id/run_id/app_id identifiers, with same-identifier prior messages pulled in automatically to resolve context.
systems.self_host: Yes — Apache-2.0 OSS (mem0ai/mem0), run entirely locally/offline with your own LLM and choice of ~20 vector-store backends. The hosted Platform is optional, not required for any core functionality.
systems.best_for: Teams wanting a drop-in, framework-agnostic memory API (works with LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, LangGraph, or the raw OpenAI SDK) that can be self-hosted for free or scaled through a metered hosted tier, without having to reason about graph structure themselves.
systems.watch: The April 2026 default algorithm switched to single-pass 'ADD-only' extraction — vendor's own words are 'one LLM call, no UPDATE/DELETE' — replacing an earlier ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP decision engine that older docs and the original mem0 paper describe; confirm which mode a given SDK/deployment version actually runs before assuming automatic conflict resolution exists (see memory_policy for what changed and what lifecycle controls exist instead).
systems.standout: Multi-signal retrieval (semantic + BM25 + entity linking) plus optional graph memory, exposed through one of the simplest APIs in the category (essentially one add()/search() call pair), and genuinely free to self-host at unlimited scale.
systems.memory_policy: As of an April 2026 default-algorithm change, new facts are added in a single LLM call with no automatic UPDATE/DELETE reconciliation against prior memories — an earlier ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP decision engine (described in the original mem0 paper) is no longer the default, so memories accumulate rather than being reconciled unless an older mode is explicitly selected. Nothing is deleted automatically. Two opt-in, Platform-only lifecycle controls exist: a per-memory expiration_date (hides a memory from search once past; the underlying data is not removed) and, since a 2026-07-31 release, 'Memory Decay' — a per-project toggle that down-weights a stale memory's relevance score by recency (floor 0.3x, never fully removed). Both are off by default, so an unmanaged deployment's memory grows forever and ranks with no recency adjustment.
systems.embedding_model: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small by default, fully configurable; embedding model and vector-store backend are decoupled, so any supported combination works via a config change, not a code change.
systems.scale_note: 62.8k GitHub stars (verified via GitHub, Aug 2026). PyPI downloads are materially higher than any figure this row can source cleanly — pepy.tech showed 38.6M+ all-time as of May 2026 with a ~4M/month run-rate per pypistats.org — so treat any specific download count here as vendor/aggregator-sourced, not independently benchmarked, until re-pulled directly from pepy.tech at publish time. Vendor frames the April 2026 algorithm rewrite explicitly as a token-efficiency/scaling fix versus the older multi-call ADD/UPDATE/DELETE approach — no independent benchmark of the new algorithm was found.
systems.integration: REST API plus Python/Node/Go SDKs; explicitly framework-agnostic, with documented integrations for LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, AutoGen, LangGraph, and raw OpenAI-SDK usage.
systems.adoption: 62.8k GitHub stars (verified via GitHub, Aug 2026). PyPI download figure could not be independently confirmed: pepy.tech showed mem0ai at 38.6M+ all-time downloads as of May 2026 already, with pypistats.org showing a ~4M/month current run-rate (implying 45M+ by Aug 2026) — the previously-stated '13M+' does not match any current source and its claimed 'verified via direct repo fetch' method is not possible (GitHub does not host PyPI download counts, and the README badge is a dynamically-rendered image with no number in the page source). $24M raised (seed + Series A; led by Basis Set Ventures, with Peak XV Partners, Kindred Ventures, GitHub Fund and Y Combinator participating).
systems.released: Founded 2023 (Y Combinator-backed); open-sourced and hosted Platform launched through 2023–2024.

systems.name: MemoryOS
systems.price_note: No pricing - Apache-2.0 open-source Python package (pip install memoryos-pro), Docker image, and MCP server only; no hosted product or managed service exists for the memory engine itself. A companion Playground web UI was open-sourced in September 2025 as a self-hosted demo, not a paid tier. Cost is entirely whatever LLM (an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint is required) and embedding provider you configure it to call.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: OS-inspired three-tier pipeline rather than a single vector index. Short-term memory (STM) is a fixed-length FIFO queue of recent dialogue pages; mid-term memory (MTM) groups pages into topic segments via a segmented-paging strategy and scores each segment with a heat value (visit frequency, interaction length, and recency); segments whose heat crosses a threshold are LLM-summarized and promoted into long-term personal memory (LPM, a persistent user profile/persona plus a knowledge base). Retrieval draws from all three tiers plus the LPM profile to assemble context, backed by a Chromadb vector store.
systems.self_host: Yes - self-hostable only, Apache-2.0, via pip (pip install memoryos-pro), a Docker image, or by running the MCP server locally; no cloud-hosted version of the memory engine exists (LLM calls still require an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint and key, configured by the operator).
systems.best_for: Teams wanting a self-hosted, research-grounded (EMNLP 2025 oral) hierarchical memory layer with an explicit heat-based promotion/eviction policy across short/mid/long-term tiers, rather than a flat vector store or a single add()/search() API.
systems.watch: Mid-term segments that never cross the heat threshold are evicted, not archived, once MTM's own capacity is exceeded - there is no separate long-term "cold storage" for low-heat content, so an infrequently-revisited topic can be lost outright rather than merely deprioritized. The project is young (repository created May 2025) and appears to be maintained by a single academic lab (BAI-LAB, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); production adoption beyond the paper's own benchmarks is not established.
systems.standout: One of few systems in this set to frame memory management explicitly as an operating-system problem - short-term, mid-term, and long-term tiers with paging-style promotion and heat-based eviction, rather than a flat add()/search() call pair or a single vector index.
systems.memory_policy: A three-tier hierarchy handles promotion and forgetting differently at each boundary. Short-term memory (STM) holds the most recent dialogue turns in a fixed-length FIFO queue; when STM's capacity is exceeded, the oldest page moves into mid-term memory (MTM), where a segmented-paging strategy groups related pages into topic segments. Each MTM segment accumulates a heat score from three factors - visit frequency, interaction length, and recency - and a segment whose heat crosses a configurable threshold is LLM-summarized and promoted into long-term personal memory (LPM, a persistent user profile/persona plus a knowledge base). When MTM's own capacity is exceeded, the segments with the lowest heat are evicted outright rather than promoted; the paper and README do not describe promoted LPM content itself being pruned or decaying further, so forgetting happens only at the mid-term eviction step, not from long-term storage once written.
systems.embedding_model: Pluggable - ships support for BAAI/bge-m3, Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as embedding options, backed by a Chromadb vector store; LLM calls (separate from embeddings) go through an OpenAI-compatible interface, so the model doing extraction can be any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
systems.scale_note: Vendor/paper-reported only - the MemoryOS paper (arXiv:2506.06326, "Memory OS of AI Agent") reports +49.11% F1 and +46.18% BLEU-1 over baselines on the LoCoMo long-term-dialogue benchmark using GPT-4o-mini. No independent benchmark or production-scale figure was found.
systems.integration: Python package plus a dedicated MCP server (three tools - add_memory, retrieve_memory, and get_user_profile) for Claude and other agent tool use; all LLM calls go through an OpenAI-compatible API interface, so OpenAI, Anthropic, Deepseek-R1, Qwen3, vLLM, or Llama Factory can all be pointed at it via base_url, decoupled from the separately-configured embedding backend.
systems.adoption: 1.5k GitHub stars, 153 forks (BAI-LAB/MemoryOS, verified via GitHub API, Aug 2026); accepted as an EMNLP 2025 oral presentation (Aug 21, 2025, per the repo's own description); cited in subsequent survey literature alongside Letta/MemGPT and A-MEM as a distinct agentic-memory paradigm (e.g. arXiv:2607.29433).
systems.released: Repository created May 30, 2025; accepted to the EMNLP 2025 main conference (oral) on August 21, 2025.

systems.name: Supermemory
systems.price_note: Free, self-hosted via the MIT-licensed single binary (curl install or npx supermemory local; no Docker, database, or config file required). Hosted platform: Free $0/mo (~$5/mo usage credit) → Pro $19/mo (~$20/mo usage credit, unlimited storage/users, 2 teammates, Google Drive/Notion/OneDrive connectors) → Max $100/mo (~$130/mo usage credit, adds Gmail/Granola connectors) → Scale $399/mo (~$600/mo usage credit, up to 10 teammates, all connectors, SOC 2/HIPAA BAA, and a listed 'self-hosted option') → custom Enterprise (air-gapped self-hosting, committed-spend pricing). The self-hosting docs describe the open-source binary itself as free with no stated limits, but the pricing page separately lists 'a self-hosted option' as a Scale-and-up feature and 'air-gapped self-hosting' as Enterprise-only - worth clarifying with the vendor which capabilities the free binary covers versus what the paid tiers add on top of self-hosting.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Hybrid vector + keyword search with, per Supermemory's own site, "sub-300ms latency" - a context-aware reranker lets a strong keyword match short-circuit a full approximate-nearest-neighbor pass rather than forcing every query through it. Facts are additionally organized into a memory graph: an UPDATES relationship links a new fact to the one it supersedes, with an isLatest flag keeping retrieval on the current fact "without erasing the past" (per Supermemory's docs). Local embeddings default to Xenova/bge-base-en-v1.5 (768-dimensional, runs fully offline).
systems.self_host: Yes - MIT-licensed, a single binary with, per vendor, zero external dependencies: "No Docker. No database to provision. No config files." An embedded graph engine and local embedding model are created automatically on first boot; the identical API is used locally (http://localhost:6767) or against the hosted platform by changing the base URL.
systems.best_for: Teams wanting a self-hostable, framework-agnostic memory API with contradiction resolution and automatic forgetting documented as first-class, named mechanisms in the API itself, rather than something built by hand on top of a raw vector store.
systems.watch: The free/self-hosted OSS path and the commercial platform's tiered "self-hosted option" are not obviously the same thing: the open binary self-hosts with no published limits, but the pricing page lists a "self-hosted option" only from the $399/mo Scale tier up (with full air-gapped deployment reserved for Enterprise) - confirm exactly which connectors, graph features, and support are actually included when self-hosting for free versus paying for the tiered "self-hosted option" before assuming parity. Contradiction resolution is described only at the level of "new fact replaces old" via the UPDATES/isLatest graph relationship; no documentation was found on how a contradiction is detected (embedding similarity vs. LLM judgment), or on any policy for facts that go stale without an explicit superseding update (only explicitly time-bound facts are forgotten automatically).
systems.standout: Combines two named, first-class mechanisms most competitors in this category document only one of: contradiction resolution (an UPDATES graph relationship with an isLatest flag) and automatic time-based forgetting of expired facts - backed by a "sub-300ms" hybrid-retrieval latency claim published on Supermemory's own site.
systems.memory_policy: Contradiction handling and forgetting are both named, documented mechanisms rather than developer-built add-ons. A new fact that supersedes an old one is linked via an UPDATES graph relationship; per Supermemory's own docs, "New fact replaces what was true before for search purposes; history can remain for audit," with an isLatest flag keeping retrieval on the current fact "without erasing the past." Two forgetting modes are documented: time-based (a temporary fact such as "meeting at 3pm today" or "exam tomorrow" is dropped once it expires) and noise filtering (casual, non-meaningful chatter is less likely to become a durable memory in the first place). No detail is published on how a contradiction is detected (embedding similarity vs. LLM judgment), and no policy is documented for a fact that simply goes stale without an explicit superseding update.
systems.embedding_model: Local by default (Xenova/bge-base-en-v1.5, 768-dimensional, runs offline with no API key); OpenAI, Google Gemini, or Ollama can be configured instead for embeddings, and Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, or llama.cpp can serve the LLM side fully offline.
systems.scale_note: 28.8k GitHub stars, 2.5k forks (supermemoryai/supermemory, verified via GitHub API, Aug 2026). Supermemory's own LongMemEval-S research page reports 95% Recall@15 (with aggregation) at roughly 720 mean tokens added to context, against baselines of 71.2% (Zep) and 60.2% (full-context, no retrieval). Other secondary aggregator sites report additional comparative figures against Mem0 and on LoCoMo that could not be traced to a primary Supermemory page and are omitted here as unverified. All performance figures are vendor-reported and self-published, not independently audited.
systems.integration: REST API plus SDKs; documented framework integrations for the Vercel AI SDK, LangChain, LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Mastra, and Agno; an MCP server (mcp.supermemory.ai) usable from Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and Windsurf; first-party connectors for Google Drive, Gmail, Notion, OneDrive, GitHub, and a web crawler.
systems.adoption: 28.8k GitHub stars, 2.5k forks (supermemoryai/supermemory, verified via GitHub API, Aug 2026); $2.6M seed round (announced October 2025, led by Susa Ventures, Browder Capital, and SF1.vc; angel investors reported by TechCrunch to include Google AI chief Jeff Dean and Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht, among others) - some secondary outlets round this to "$3M."
systems.released: Repository created February 27, 2024; company founded by Dhravya Shah.

systems.name: FalkorDB + GraphRAG-SDK
systems.licence: GraphRAG-SDK: Apache-2.0. FalkorDB database itself: Server Side Public License v1 (SSPLv1) — source-available, not OSI-approved.
systems.price_note: GraphRAG-SDK: $0, open source. FalkorDB Cloud: free tier (100MB RAM, no card); Startup tier from $73/mo (1GB RAM, $0.10/GB-RAM/hr); Pro tier from $350/mo (8GB RAM, HA, usage-based per-GB-RAM/hr and per-core/hr pricing published with an online calculator, not quote-only); Enterprise/BYOC custom.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: LLM-driven entity/relationship extraction per document chunk (two-step: local NER model finds entities, then LLM verifies and extracts relationships), constrained to either a code-defined GraphSchema (EntityType/RelationType) or, absent a schema, an SDK-provided default set of 11 entity types — not true open-world/unrestricted extraction, contrary to the vendor-neutral phrase 'open-world extraction' used here. Entity resolution is exact-match dedup by normalized name+type, plus an optional three-tier LLM-verified resolution strategy (embedding similarity ≥0.95 auto-merges, 0.80-0.95 goes to LLM verification) for merging ambiguous surface forms. Retrieval hybridizes vector chunk search, full-text search, optional LLM-generated Cypher queries (text-to-Cypher, bypasses the reranker), and relationship-embedding expansion (1-2 hop plus direct RELATES vector search), reranked by cosine similarity to the question.
systems.self_host: Yes. FalkorDB is a single-binary graph database (Redis-module architecture, GraphBLAS-backed sparse matrices) self-hostable under SSPLv1 terms; GraphRAG-SDK runs against it or FalkorDB Cloud.
systems.best_for: Teams wanting a fast, purpose-built-for-GraphRAG graph database (not a generic graph DB retrofitted for it) with a first-party SDK covering extraction, ontology, and retrieval.
systems.watch: SSPLv1 is a real licence-catch, not a formality — it specifically targets 'offering the software as a service.' A team planning to resell FalkorDB-backed memory as a hosted product should get legal sign-off; GraphRAG-SDK's Apache-2.0 license does not cover the storage engine it depends on.
systems.standout: The only system in this set that is itself a purpose-built graph database (not a library layered on Neo4j), with GraphRAG-specific tooling shipped as a first-party SDK.
systems.memory_policy: No automatic decay/forgetting is documented. Updates go through an idempotent rollforward-cutover: changed content is written to a hidden pending document, then swapped in atomically via a single Cypher statement — crash-safe incremental re-ingestion rather than a temporal fact-invalidation policy. Per-agent/per-tenant isolation is via separate named graphs within one FalkorDB instance, not via in-graph forgetting.
systems.embedding_model: Pluggable via LiteLLM across 100+ providers (OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock, Ollama, etc.); docs example default is openai/text-embedding-3-large.
systems.scale_note: GraphBLAS sparse-matrix engine targets low-latency graph queries; cloud tiers scale from 100MB (free) to custom Enterprise/BYOC.
systems.integration: Python SDK (graphrag-sdk on PyPI); FalkorDB itself has client libraries for Python, Node.js, Go, Java, Rust and speaks a Cypher-like query language; also used as a storage backend option by Graphiti and other GraphRAG stacks.
systems.adoption: Named explicitly as a supported storage backend in Graphiti's own docs; GraphRAG-SDK is used in FalkorDB's own published multi-tenant agent-memory reference architectures.
systems.released: FalkorDB launched 2023 (fork of RedisGraph following its end-of-life); GraphRAG-SDK released as its GenAI tooling layer.

systems.name: Graphiti (getzep/graphiti)
systems.price_note: Free, open source, self-hosted: $0. Optional hosted access via Zep Cloud from $125/mo ($104/mo billed annually) after a 10,000-credit/mo free tier; credits meter ingested episode bytes, while retrieval, storage, threads, users, and graph storage itself consume zero credits.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: LLM-driven entity/relationship extraction per ingested 'episode' (message, doc chunk, or JSON) against either a developer-defined Pydantic-model ontology (prescribed) or an open/learned schema. Retrieval fuses semantic (embedding) search, BM25 keyword search, and graph traversal/BFS expansion from seed nodes, reranked, with support for point-in-time queries against the temporal validity windows.
systems.self_host: Yes — a Python library you run yourself against a graph backend of your choice: Neo4j 5.26+, FalkorDB 1.1.2+ (including embedded 'Lite'), Amazon Neptune (+ OpenSearch Serverless for full-text), or Kuzu 0.11.2 (flagged in Graphiti's own docs as deprecated/unmaintained upstream — avoid for new deployments).
systems.best_for: Teams that want the bi-temporal knowledge-graph engine itself, as an embeddable library, rather than adopting a managed memory product wholesale.
systems.watch: No automatic decay: invalidated facts accumulate forever unless you build your own pruning job. The Kuzu embedded backend is explicitly flagged deprecated/unmaintained in Graphiti's own docs.
systems.standout: Bi-temporal fact invalidation (t_valid/t_invalid) backed by a published, cited architecture paper, and the only system here offering four interchangeable graph-backend targets.
systems.memory_policy: Bi-temporal: every edge carries both valid-time (valid_at/invalid_at — when the fact was true in the world) and transaction-time (created_at/expired_at — when it was ingested/superseded). New episodes are checked against existing edges via combined semantic, keyword, and graph search; a contradicting fact gets the old edge invalidated (its expired_at is set and invalid_at recorded) rather than deleted, so the graph can answer 'what was believed and when' and never serves a stale fact as current. There is no automatic decay/expiry — invalidated edges persist as history forever unless the operator builds their own pruning job.
systems.embedding_model: Pluggable via an LLM-client abstraction: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (default), Azure OpenAI, Google Gemini embedding-001, Voyage, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp) for local/self-hosted embeddings.
systems.scale_note: Scale is inherited from whichever backend it's pointed at (Neo4j/FalkorDB/Neptune); Zep's hosted Context Lake advertises enterprise-scale deployment (cloud, BYOK, BYOC).
systems.integration: Python library (pip install graphiti-core); ships an MCP server for Claude/agent tool use; framework-agnostic, wired into LangChain, LlamaIndex, and custom agent loops via its own API.
systems.adoption: 29.7k GitHub stars (verified via GitHub API); is the engine behind Zep's commercial Context Lake platform; reference implementation for the 'Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory' paper (arXiv 2501.13956).

systems.name: Memary
systems.price_note: Free and open source: $0, self-hosted only — no hosted/managed offering was found.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: A ReAct agent plans and calls a graph-search tool that queries existing entities/nodes in the knowledge graph; if no related entity is found, it falls back to an external search (Perplexity) and writes the result back into the graph, growing it incrementally.
systems.self_host: Yes, self-hosted only — you run your own Neo4j or FalkorDB instance.
systems.best_for: Small teams or hobbyists wanting a minimal, fully-readable reference implementation of a frequency+recency graph-memory policy to study or fork, rather than a production platform.
systems.watch: Last commit/merge to main was PR #61 ('FalkorDB Multi Graph ability') on 2024-10-18 (repo pushed_at: 2024-10-22T00:46:00Z per the GitHub API) — there is no evidence of a September 2025 merge anywhere in the repo's history. Three community pull requests (#65, #66, #67, opened 2026-05-15 through 2026-06-27) sit open and unmerged, and issue #64 (opened 2025-01-02) remains open — none addressed by a maintainer. Not formally archived (archived: false), but there has been no maintainer commit activity in nearly two years. Verify at github.com/kingjulio8238/Memary/commits/main before betting production work on it.
systems.standout: The simplest, most readable open-source implementation of a 'frequency + recency = what's worth remembering' policy in this category.
systems.memory_policy: Two-part model: a 'Memory Stream' logs every entity and timestamp the agent has encountered (breadth of knowledge), and an 'Entity Knowledge Store' tracks reference frequency and recency per entity (depth of knowledge), which together rank what's most worth surfacing. Long chat history is handled by summarization/compression rather than deletion. No explicit automatic decay/forgetting mechanism is documented — recency is used for ranking retrieval, not for removing old memories.
systems.embedding_model: LLM-dependent rather than a separate embedding step: Llama 3 (8B/40B via Ollama) or GPT-3.5-turbo for reasoning/extraction, LLaVA or GPT-4-vision-preview for its vision tool, Perplexity's mistral-7b-instruct for external search fallback.
systems.scale_note: Designed as a single-agent/small-scale reference implementation; no published benchmarks on graph size or throughput were found.
systems.integration: Python library; a ReAct-style agent loop with a graph-search tool plus a computer-vision tool (LLaVa) and a geocoding/maps tool; supports either Neo4j or FalkorDB as the graph backend.
systems.adoption: 2.6k GitHub stars (kingjulio8238/Memary); covered on Hacker News at launch.

systems.name: Neo4j Agent Memory (NAMS)
