systems.licence: Apache-2.0 (neo4j-agent-memory library/service code); requires a Neo4j 5.20+ backend — Neo4j Community Edition (GPLv3) is free to self-host, Neo4j Enterprise/Aura is commercial.
systems.price_note: Library + self-hosted Neo4j Community: $0 (Apache-2.0 + GPLv3 free tier). Hosted NAMS console (memory.neo4jlabs.com, Neo4j Aura-backed) pricing was not publicly listed as of this research — it is an early-access Labs project.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Multi-stage entity extraction (spaCy, GLiNER, and LLM-based) plus GLiREL for relationship extraction; hybrid vector + full-text search over the graph, with optional geospatial queries and background entity enrichment from Wikipedia/Diffbot.
systems.self_host: Yes — self-hosted Bolt connection to your own Neo4j instance (air-gapped capable, write-Cypher access) or Neo4j Aura; also offered as a hosted NAMS service with no database to run yourself.
systems.best_for: Teams already on Neo4j, or wanting the most explicit multi-tier (short/long/reasoning) memory architecture with a documented entity schema, rather than one flat fact graph.
systems.watch: This is a Neo4j Labs project — Neo4j's own framing is 'experimental and community supported,' not a GA product with an SLA, and hosted pricing is not yet published. Confirm current status before depending on it for production.
systems.standout: The only system here with three named, separately-modeled memory tiers (short-term/long-term/reasoning) in one schema, plus an adopt_existing_graph() path to bring an existing Neo4j graph under memory management.
systems.memory_policy: Three explicit memory tiers: short-term (per-session messages), long-term (entities/preferences/facts under a 'POLE+O' schema — Persons, Objects, Locations, Events + Organizations), and reasoning memory (tool-use/decision traces linked to entities via :TOUCHED audit edges). Conflict resolution runs through automatic entity deduplication/resolution against the POLE+O schema, not temporal fact-invalidation. No published automatic decay/forgetting policy — consolidation is offered as an operator-invoked primitive, not a background process.
systems.embedding_model: Provider-agnostic: native support for OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex AI, and sentence-transformers (for local/air-gapped use); broader coverage (Cohere, Voyage, Groq, Together, Mistral, Ollama) via a LiteLLM fallback.
systems.scale_note: Inherits Neo4j's own scale characteristics; the hosted NAMS console runs on Neo4j Aura.
systems.integration: Python and TypeScript SDKs; MCP server exposing 6–16 memory tools; framework integrations for LangChain, Pydantic AI, Google ADK, and CrewAI; a create-context-graph CLI for full-stack scaffolding.
systems.adoption: 405 GitHub stars (neo4j-labs/agent-memory); showcased via the public 'Lenny's Memory' demo (300+ podcast episodes as a browsable knowledge graph) and Neo4j's developer blog.
systems.released: 2026 — Neo4j Labs, explicitly framed by Neo4j as an early-access incubation project ('opened up early... not a big-bang launch').

systems.name: WhyHow.ai Knowledge Graph Studio + SDK
systems.price_note: Open-source SDK/Studio: $0 (MIT), self-hosted. The README advertises a cloud-hosted Knowledge Graph Studio UI, but as of this check (Aug 2026) that product page (whyhow.ai/knowledge-graph-studio) returns HTTP 404 and the company's current website has no mention of Knowledge Graph Studio, the SDK, or knowledge graphs at all — the cloud offering appears discontinued.
systems.retrieval_mechanics: Rule-based entity parsing against a developer-defined schema, modular graph construction from ingested documents, and schema-aware retrieval intended to reduce the noisy/ungrounded extraction common to fully-automatic LLM graph-builders.
systems.self_host: Yes — SDK and Knowledge Graph Studio are open source (MIT) and self-hostable. A cloud-hosted version was previously offered on the company website; that product page now 404s and appears discontinued (see watch).
systems.best_for: Teams wanting tight, developer-authored control over what schema the graph is allowed to have (fewer hallucinated node/edge types), over letting an LLM freely invent an ontology.
systems.watch: The company behind this project (whyhow.ai) has fully pivoted its live website to an unrelated AI litigation/legal-tech product (plaintiff case sourcing for mass torts and class actions) with zero mention of Knowledge Graph Studio, the SDK, or knowledge graphs anywhere on it, and the README's own link to the cloud-hosted Studio product page (whyhow.ai/knowledge-graph-studio) now 404s. GitHub shows no commits to knowledge-graph-studio or the whyhow SDK since Dec 25, 2024 (~20 months), and an open issue titled 'Maintained?' (#24, filed Sep 22, 2025, asking exactly whether to invest time in this) has received zero maintainer response as of this check. Treat this as an orphaned open-source snapshot from a company that has moved to a different business, not an actively supported product — the code is still usable/self-hostable under MIT, but do not expect fixes, releases, or the advertised cloud tier.
systems.standout: The one system in this set built explicitly around a small, developer-controlled schema rather than open-world LLM extraction — optimizing for predictability over automatic breadth.
systems.memory_policy: Schema-controlled ('rule-based') entity/relationship extraction — the developer defines the schema up front rather than letting an LLM freely infer an open-world ontology, pitched as keeping graphs small, predictable, and easier to maintain. No documented conflict-resolution (fact invalidation) or decay/forgetting mechanism was found in the material surfaced here — this reads closer to a knowledge-graph construction/RAG toolkit than a system with an explicit memory-lifecycle policy.
systems.embedding_model: Not pinned to a specific default in the surfaced docs — schema-guided extraction is LLM-driven with standard OpenAI-compatible model configuration.
systems.scale_note: Not established from the sources reviewed.
systems.integration: Python SDK (whyhow-ai/whyhow) and a REST API; the Studio UI is available self-hosted from the open-source repo. A cloud-hosted Studio UI was previously advertised via the README but its linked product page now 404s and is absent from the company's current site — treat the hosted option as discontinued. Positioned as complementary to vector-only RAG stacks.
systems.adoption: 927 GitHub stars (knowledge-graph-studio), 672 stars (knowledge-table), 128 stars (whyhow SDK).
systems.released: Company founded circa 2023; Knowledge Graph Studio and SDK released through 2023–2024.

corrections.claim: Cognee is the only system in this catalog with an explicit, named forget() operation and a continuous confidence re-weighting loop as a first-class part of the API.
corrections.reality: mem0's own row in this catalog documents an explicit delete()/delete_all() API plus a named Memory Decay feature (shipped 2026-07-31) that continuously down-weights a stale memory's relevance score by recency. Cognee's forget() is more granular in scope (item-level, dataset-level, memory-only, or account-wide) and its re-weighting considers importance, frequency, and feedback together rather than recency alone - genuinely distinct, but not unique in kind.

gaps: Cognee is architecturally both a memory-framework and a graph-memory system (it unifies graph, vector, and relational storage in one pipeline) — research initially produced two separate rows, one per category; they were merged into a single memory-framework row with graph-structured in its facets, rather than published as two entries under one name.

Letta's initial research described its superseded legacy server (Postgres+pgvector archival memory); a follow-up research pass corrected the row to describe the current flagship product, Letta Code, and its git-backed Context Repository / MemFS memory architecture.

This catalog does not attempt to be exhaustive — it covers 25 systems (26 found by research, minus one row lost to the Cognee merge above) across three categories (13 vector-db, 7 memory-framework, 5 graph-memory), not every vector database or memory framework that exists.
